title: UK Inflation Falls to 15-Month Low as Oil Prices Cool, but Rebound Looms
excerpt: Consumer prices rose 2.6% in June, beating forecasts, though economists warn higher energy bills and renewed Middle East tensions will push inflation back up by autumn.
body:
• UK consumer price inflation dropped to 2.6% in June from 2.8% in May, the lowest reading since March 2025 and below the 2.7% economists had forecast.
  • Falling fuel prices — driven by the brief US-Iran ceasefire and lower global oil costs — were the main factor, with diesel down 10.7p per litre in a single month.
  • Economists expect June to mark the low point for this year, with inflation likely climbing toward 3.3–3.75% by autumn as Ofgem's 13% energy price cap hike takes effect.
  • The Bank of England is widely expected to hold its key interest rate at 3.75% at its July 30 meeting.

Britain's annual inflation rate fell to 2.6% in June, the Office for National Statistics reported Wednesday, dropping below the 2.7% consensus forecast and marking the lowest reading in 15 months. The decline from May's 2.8% was driven primarily by a sharp retreat in fuel prices after the tentative US-Iran ceasefire in June brought temporary relief to global energy markets.

What Drove the Drop

Motor fuel was the biggest single drag on the headline number. Diesel prices fell 10.7p to 176.4p per litre between May and June, while petrol dropped 2.1p to 155.3p per litre. Energy inflation decelerated to 5.7% from 7.4% the previous month as the cessation of hostilities in the Middle East briefly cooled global crude prices.

Food prices added to the downward pull. Annual grocery inflation eased to 1.7% from 2.2%, the lowest since August 2024. Grant Fitzner, the ONS's chief economist, noted that prices for chocolate, margarine, and beef all fell, while summer sales brought bigger-than-usual clothing discounts.

A Brief Reprieve for the New Government

The data lands in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first full week in office. Burnham has moved quickly on cost-of-living priorities, announcing that VAT on electricity bills will be removed from October — a measure officials say could shave 0.1 percentage points off annual inflation — and capping most single bus fares in England at £2.

""Falling inflation is news families want to hear but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need," he said."

Chancellor John Healey welcomed the figures. "Falling inflation is news families want to hear but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need," he said. The ONS also reported this week that government borrowing in June came in at £16 billion, nearly £5 billion below the same month last year.

Why the Gains May Not Last

Economists are nearly unanimous that June will mark this year's inflation trough. Ofgem lifted the household energy price cap by 13% at the start of July, and oil prices have climbed sharply after President Trump declared the tentative US-Iran ceasefire "over" and airstrikes resumed. Brent crude rose above $92 a barrel on Wednesday.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, warned that "rebounding energy prices, a wave of inflation coming through supply chains and a pickup in food prices will probably drive inflation to a peak of 3.3% in the autumn, even after the removal of VAT on energy bills." The Bank of England's own forecasts project headline CPI reaching approximately 3.75% in the fourth quarter.

What It Means for Interest Rates

Core inflation — stripping out volatile food and energy — held steady at 2.6%, while services inflation edged down to 3.6% from 3.7%. Markets fully expect the Bank of England to hold rates at 3.75% when its Monetary Policy Committee meets on July 30. Before the Iran conflict, the central bank had anticipated inflation falling below its 2% target; markets now price in two rate hikes by March 2027 instead.

"June's peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil-and-gas prices helped cool CPI inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new prime minister's premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived."

— Charlotte O'Leary, associate economist, National Institute of Economic and Social Research

The UK's pullback mirrored a broader trend. Eurozone inflation fell to 2.8% from 3.2%, while US CPI cooled to 3.5% from 4.2%, as global fossil fuel prices temporarily retreated following hopes of a lasting reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

For Indian-origin professionals and families in the UK, the near-term outlook is mixed. Lower grocery and fuel bills offer immediate relief, but the expected autumn rebound means household budgets will remain under pressure heading into winter.
